title: Fortified legislature
primary_topics: Three-branch DAP-aftermath trilogy capper August 31, 2014 -- third of three consecutive Sundays (with A403 Aug 17 and A402 Aug 24)
Parliamentary-vs-presidential separation-of-powers framing opening -- parliamentary chief executives owe absolute loyalty to parliament, deposable on confidence-loss

European judiciary subdivisions: supreme courts (civil/criminal/commercial) + constitutional courts (constitutional issues) + high administrative courts (executive-agency appeals); cannot normally reverse parliament except constitutional courts

Presidential-system framing: legislature is repository of sovereign will but president (direct vote) gets enormous powers eclipsing lawmakers; hundreds of legislators must collegially deliberate vs president acts alone and fast with Cabinet
1936-Charter presidential-dominance vs 1987-Constitution fortified-Congress thesis (back-ref to A403 Aug 17)

Power-of-the-purse anchored in constitutional citation: 'No public money shall be paid out of the treasury, except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law'; even Congress cannot pass another law 'authorizing any transfer of appropriations'

One limited exception: power of augmentation (renamed DAP by PNoy) -- president/SP/Speaker/CJ/ConCom-heads may 'by law' augment items in GAA for their respective offices from savings in other items; back-ref to July 6/20/27 columns (A407/A405/A404)

Congressional checks: (1) easier impeachment thresholds reduced -- 1936 required 2/3 representatives + 3/4 senators; 1987 needs only 1/3 + 2/3; two grounds added (graft+corruption, betrayal-of-public-trust) to original four (culpable violation of Constitution, treason, bribery, other high crimes)

More fortifications: (2) department heads can't be banned from probes -- only executive-session for security/public-interest reasons under PNoy; (3) lawmaker criminal-arrest immunity extended to offenses under 6 years while Congress in session (previously only civil arrests); (4) emergency powers conferred on president 'shall cease upon next adjournment'
Final fortification: (5) Senate concurrence required for 'international agreements' not just treaties -- broadens treaty-clause scope; martial-law power constraints back-reference to A403

stances.claim: In most democracies, the legislature is the most powerful branch of government because it represents and expresses the sovereign will of the people -- especially true in parliamentary systems where chief executives (prime ministers) are elected by and owe absolute loyalty to parliament; tripartite separation of powers finds no application in parliamentary governments

In many European countries, the judiciary is inferior to parliament -- judicial power normally divided among many high courts: supreme courts (civil/criminal/commercial), constitutional courts (constitutional issues), high administrative courts (executive-agency appeals like equivalents of BIR, BSP, SEC); normally these high courts cannot reverse parliament, save for constitutional courts in exceptional cases

In presidential systems, the legislature is also considered the repository of sovereign will, but because the chief executive (president) is elected by direct vote of the people and is thus not totally beholden to the legislature, he/she is constitutionally-granted enormous powers that easily eclipse the lawmakers' -- since legislative power is exercised by hundreds of elected representatives and senators who must first collegially deliberate before they can act, the president becomes the most powerful official, easily outmaneuvering and overpowering the legislators

Presidential dominance characterized our 1936 Charter; but as CJ discussed Aug 17 (A403), the 1987 Constitution weakened the presidency -- to curtail executive abuses and excesses, it fortified Congress and empowered the Supreme Court; legislative power is simply the power to make laws and to modify or repeal them, and the most important law is the General Appropriations Act (GAA) or budget enacted yearly

To fortify congressional control over the public purse, the 1987 Constitution expressly provides: 'No public money shall be paid out of the treasury, except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law'; and after such appropriation is made by law via the GAA, not even Congress is authorized by the Charter to pass another law 'authorizing any transfer of appropriations' -- there is one very limited exception, the power of augmentation (referred to by PNoy as DAP), discussed extensively in CJ's three July columns (A407, A405, A404); the new Charter has tightly barricaded the congressional power over the purse, as shown by the DAP decision

Aside from martial-law constraints (A403), the new Charter granted Congress extensive powers to check the presidency: (1) made it easier to remove presidents -- 1936 required 2/3 representatives to impeach and 3/4 senators to convict; 1987 needs only 1/3 and 2/3 respectively; added two new grounds (graft+corruption, betrayal-of-public-trust) to the original four (culpable violation of Constitution, treason, bribery, other high crimes)

More congressional checks: (2) department heads can no longer be banned from congressional probes -- under PNoy's 1987 framework they may be heard in executive session for security/public-interest reasons but appearance cannot be banned, unlike 1936 which let presidents prevent attendance by written statement; (3) lawmakers' arrest-immunity extended from civil-only (1936) to also include criminal arrests for offenses punishable by under 6 years 'while Congress is in session'; (4) emergency powers conferred on the president 'shall cease upon the next adjournment' of Congress

Finally, (5) under the old Charter, treaties could be entered into by the president provided 2/3 of all senators concur; under the new one, even 'international agreements' need 2/3 vote of the Senate -- broadening the treaty-clause scope to capture executive-only agreements that would otherwise bypass Senate review

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers the third installment of his three-branch DAP-aftermath trilogy (August 31, 2014; companions A403 Aug 17 'Weakened presidency' and A402 Aug 24 'Transformation of SC justices'). Legislative supremacy: in most democracies, the legislature is the most powerful branch of government because it represents and expresses the sovereign will of the people. This is especially true in parliamentary systems, where the chief executives (prime ministers) are elected by and owe absolute loyalty to parliament; once parliament loses confidence in them for whatever reason, they are deposed. The tripartite separation of powers finds no application in parliamentary governments. In many European countries, the judiciary is inferior to parliament. Judicial power is normally divided among many high courts: their supreme courts review civil, criminal and commercial decisions of lower courts; their constitutional courts adjudicate constitutional issues; and their high administrative courts decide appeals from executive agencies (equivalents of our BIR, BSP, SEC). Normally, these high courts cannot reverse actions of parliament, save for the constitutional courts in exceptional cases. In presidential systems, the legislature is also considered the repository of the sovereign will, but because the chief executive (president) is elected by direct vote of the people and is thus not totally beholden to the legislature, he/she is constitutionally-granted enormous powers that easily eclipse the lawmakers'. Since legislative power is exercised by hundreds of elected representatives and senators who must first collegially deliberate and agree before they can act, the president becomes the most powerful official -- assisted by a Cabinet and other officials, the president can act alone and fast, easily outmaneuvering and overpowering the legislators. Power of the purse: presidential dominance characterized our 1936 Charter. But as CJ discussed on Aug 17 (A403), the 1987 Constitution weakened the presidency -- to curtail executive abuses and excesses, it fortified Congress and empowered the SC. Legislative power is simply the power to make laws and to modify or repeal them. The most important law is the General Appropriations Act (GAA) or budget which is enacted yearly. To fortify congressional control over the public purse, the 1987 Constitution expressly provides: 'No public money shall be paid out of the treasury, except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law.' And after such appropriation is 'made by law' via the GAA, not even Congress is authorized by the Charter to pass another law 'authorizing any transfer of appropriations.' There is one very limited exception: the president (or Senate president, or House speaker, or chief justice or the heads of the constitutional commissions) 'may, by law (passed by Congress), be authorized to augment any item in the GAA for their respective offices from savings in other items of their respective appropriations.' This exception, called the power of augmentation and referred to by PNoy as DAP, had been discussed extensively in CJ's three columns last July 6, 20 and 27 (A407/A405/A404), and CJ will not belabor them now. Suffice it to say that our new Charter had tightly barricaded the congressional power over the purse and limited presidential intervention, as shown by the DAP decision of the SC. Other legislative fortifications: in his Aug 17 column (A403), CJ already discussed the stringent legislative limitations on the martial law powers of the president, making it impossible for any chief executive to become a dictator under the new Constitution, unlike under the old one which Marcos used as basis for his oxymoron 'constitutional authoritarianism.' Aside from this, the new Charter granted Congress extensive powers to check the presidency, some of which are: (1) It made it easier for Congress to remove presidents (and other impeachable officials) from their office -- the 1936 Charter required two-thirds vote of all representatives to impeach and three-fourths vote of all senators to convict, but under the new one, only one-third of all representatives and only two-thirds of all senators, respectively, are needed; the old Charter provided four grounds for impeachment (culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, and other high crimes) and the new Charter added two more (graft and corruption, betrayal of public trust). (2) Under the 1936 Charter, department heads may be prevented from attending congressional probes 'when the public interest shall require... and the President shall so state in writing' -- however, under the new one, 'when the security of the State or the public interest so requires and the President so states in writing, their appearance shall be conducted in executive session,' but cannot be banned. (3) Under the old Charter, lawmakers were exempted only from civil arrests, but under the new one, the privilege was extended to criminal arrests for offenses punishable by not more than six years imprisonment 'while Congress is in session.' (4) Under both Constitutions, Congress may, by law, confer emergency powers on the president to carry out a declared national policy, but under the new one, such powers 'shall cease upon the next adjournment' of Congress. (5) Under the old Charter, treaties may be entered into by the president provided two-thirds of all the senators concur -- under the new one, even 'international agreements' need two-thirds vote of the Senate.
